dynasties.name: Rashidun
dynasties.summary: The four caliphs who succeeded the Prophet ﷺ ruled from Madinah and then Kufa, and in thirty years carried the community from the Arabian peninsula to Persia, the Levant and Egypt.
contributions: Consolidation of the community after the death of the Prophet ﷺ, and the collection of the Qur'anic text under Abu Bakr and Uthman.
Foundation of the garrison cities of Kufa, Basra and Fustat, the earliest centres of hadith transmission.
Establishment of the diwan and the administrative practice of the conquests, later formalised by the Umayyads.

dynasties.name: Umayyad
dynasties.summary: The first hereditary caliphate ruled from Damascus and carried the Muslim world from the Atlantic coast of Iberia to the borders of China within ninety years.
contributions: Administrative reform under Abd al-Malik: Arabic in the state registers and a distinct Islamic coinage.
Monumental architecture: the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem and the Great Mosque of Damascus.
The provincial framework, postal service and army registers on which the Abbasid state was later built.

dynasties.name: Abbasid
dynasties.religion: Islam (Sunni, with Ismaili and Twelver minorities)
dynasties.summary: The Abbasid caliphate moved the centre of the Muslim world to Iraq and presided over the period in which the hadith corpus was collected, criticised and written down.
contributions: Patronage of translation and the sciences at the court in Baghdad, including the House of Wisdom under al-Ma'mun.
The classical age of hadith scholarship: the compilations of al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah were produced under Abbasid rule.
Administration, taxation and urban planning on Sasanian models, and the dinar as a stable standard of exchange.

dynasties.name: Fatimid
dynasties.government: Hereditary caliphate with a centralised chancery
dynasties.summary: The Fatimids, claiming descent from the Prophet's ﷺ daughter Fatimah, ruled Ifriqiya and then Egypt from the new city of Cairo, and contested the Abbasid caliphate across the Muslim world.
contributions: Foundation of Cairo and of al-Azhar as a centre of learning and of the Ismaili mission (da'wa).
A chancery and ceremonial court whose practice was inherited by the Ayyubid and Mamluk sultanates.
Trade and diplomacy across the Mediterranean, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean.

dynasties.name: Seljuk
dynasties.typeNote: Sultanate under the nominal Abbasid caliph
dynasties.summary: The Seljuk sultans took over the eastern Abbasid lands and Anatolia, protected the Sunni caliphate and sponsored the madrasa as the institution of Sunni learning.
contributions: The Nizamiyya madrasas, above all in Baghdad, which organised Sunni legal and hadith teaching.
Permanent Turkmen settlement of Anatolia after Manzikert (1071), the demographic base of later Anatolian states.
Persian as the language of administration and literature across the eastern Islamic world.

dynasties.name: Ayyubid
dynasties.typeNote: Sultanate of a confederated ruling family
dynasties.government: Sultanate, with rule shared among the Ayyubid family
dynasties.summary: The Ayyubid sultanate, founded by Salah al-Din, ended the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt, recovered Jerusalem and held the Muslim Levant against the crusader states.
contributions: Recovery of Jerusalem after Hattin (1187) and the treaties that reopened pilgrimage for Muslims and Christians.
Endowments and building in Cairo, Damascus and Jerusalem, including the fortification of the citadel of Cairo.
Patronage of Sunni scholarship, among it the teaching of hadith in the madrasas of Egypt and Syria.

dynasties.name: Mamluk
dynasties.summary: The Mamluk sultans of Cairo stopped the Mongols at Ayn Jalut, removed the last crusader strongholds and kept the Abbasid caliphate alive in Cairo as a title under their protection.
contributions: Military check on Mongol expansion west of Iraq after 1260.
The great Mamluk building programme of Cairo: mosques, madrasas and hospitals endowed in perpetuity.
Custody of the Hejaz and the pilgrimage routes, and a trade system linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean.
sources: Abu al-Fida, al-Mukhtasar fi Akhbar al-Bashar

dynasties.name: Ottoman
dynasties.religion: Islam (Sunni, with recognised Christian and Jewish communities)
dynasties.government: Sultanate with an imperial bureaucracy and shari'a courts
dynasties.summary: The Ottoman sultanate grew from a frontier beylik in north-western Anatolia into an empire ruling the eastern Mediterranean, the Balkans and the Hejaz, and held the caliphate from 1517 until the institution was abolished in 1924.
contributions: Law and administration: the kanun-names of Mehmed II and Suleiman I, and the office of the shaykh al-islam.
Architecture and urban life, above all the work of the architect Sinan in Istanbul and the endowments of the imperial mosques.
Custody of the two sanctuaries and of the pilgrimage, and the Ottoman school system that carried hadith teaching into the modern period.

dynasties.name: Safavid
dynasties.government: Shahdom with a Persian bureaucracy and a Turkic military elite
dynasties.summary: The Safavids united Persia under a single dynasty and made Twelver Shi'ism the religion of the state, giving the region a distinct political and religious identity.
contributions: Establishment of Twelver Shi'ism as the state religion and the organisation of its scholarly class.
Isfahan as an imperial capital, with the Naqsh-e Jahan square, its mosques and its bazaars.
Persian as the language of administration and of a renewed literary and philosophical tradition.
sources: Iskandar Beg Munshi, Tarikh-i Alam-ara-yi Abbasi

dynasties.name: Mughal
dynasties.religion: Islam (Sunni, with a large non-Muslim population)
dynasties.government: Empire with a mansabdari military-administrative system
dynasties.summary: The Mughal emperors ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from Delhi and Agra, and their courts produced some of the finest architecture and manuscript art of the Muslim world.
contributions: Administration: the mansabdari system of ranked office, revenue settlement and a Persian-language chancery.
Architecture of the imperial cities: Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort at Delhi.
Court libraries and manuscript workshops, and the hadith scholarship of the Indian madrasas.
